hook.en: Two batsmen both average 50 runs. One scores between 40 and 60 every match; the other swings between 25 and 75. The average cannot tell them apart. A measure of dispersion can.

objectives.en: Explain the meaning and need for measures of dispersion
Calculate the range and the coefficient of range

narration.en: Two batsmen both average 50 runs. One scores between 40 and 60 every match; the other swings between 25 and 75. The average cannot tell them apart. A measure of dispersion can.

body.en: Dispersion is the extent to which the values of a series differ from one another or from their average. An average describes the centre of the data; a measure of dispersion describes the scatter. It tells us how far the average represents the data, lets us compare the consistency of two series, and is the basis of further methods such as correlation. Absolute measures are in the units of the data (rupees, runs); relative measures, or coefficients, are pure numbers that allow series in different units or with different averages to be compared.

points.en: Absolute: range, quartile deviation, mean deviation, standard deviation
Relative: coefficients of these, and the coefficient of variation
Good measure: easy, uses all values, not unduly affected by extremes

body.en: The range is the difference between the largest (H) and the smallest (L) value. In a grouped series, take the upper limit of the highest class and the lower limit of the lowest class. The coefficient of range is (H − L)/(H + L). The range is simple and quick, so it is used in quality control and to report daily price movements, but it depends only on the two extreme values and ignores everything in between.

points.en: Merit: simple; demerit: based on extremes only
